name_ru: Фэн Хуан Дань Цун Хун Ча
processing: Dancong-type leaf taken to full oxidation as a black tea instead of the region's usual partial oxidation. Little is documented on the details.
harvest_season: Little is documented for the black version; Dancong leaf is usually picked from spring on.
appearance_dry: Long, dark twisted strips, in keeping with the long leaf of Dancong bushes.
taste_profile: Smooth and rich, by one seller's description. The appeal of the idea is Dancong's fragrance in a softer black tea, though how much of it survives varies.

brewing.notes: Use Dancong caution: short steeps, since the leaf can turn sharp if left too long.

vintage_note: Usually sold by harvest year as a small-batch recent tea. Since this is a side product of an oolong region, details on cultivar and season depend on the maker, so ask for them.
description:
The Fenghuang area around Chaozhou in eastern Guangdong is famous for Dancong oolong, known for a wide range of named aromas. This tea uses that same mountain's leaf but finishes it as a black tea.

Little is documented about how it is made. In principle the leaf is oxidised fully rather than partly, which trades some of the high floral top notes of oolong for a rounder, sweeter body.

A smooth, rich cup is the claim. Brew it with short steeps as you would a Dancong oolong, then taste it next to the oolong from the same area if you can.

This is a niche tea, not a recognised class with its own grades. A seller who can name the cultivar and season is a better sign than any fancy name.
history: Little is documented about this black version, and no reliable date for its first production is on record. It sits beside Fenghuang Dancong oolong, a tradition whose single-bush picking is described as taking shape in the late Qing.
